_doc: Phase 379. One row per item where the nano-ros user API does NOT correspond
to the ROS 2 client library it mirrors. Written by hand; read by
`scripts/api-parity.py --check`, which fails on any non-matching row that has
no entry here.
Key is '<lang>:<normalized item>' exactly as the report prints it, where lang
is one of c / cpp / rust. Run the report to get the spelling; do not guess it.
verdict is one of:
divergence  we changed it and a PLATFORM CONSTRAINT is why. `why` must name
the constraint (no_std, no exceptions, no allocator, no runtime
env, single-threaded transport) -- not a preference. This is the
only sanctioned reason to differ (RFC-0036).
extension   we add it because an RTOS scenario needs it; ROS 2 has none.
declined    ROS 2 has it, we deliberately do not, with the reason.
gap         ROS 2 has it, we should too, nobody has done it. A gap is a
legitimate entry -- the point is that it is written down.
rename      the names differ and OURS is the one that should change. A
rename with no platform reason costs the drop-in claim for
nothing, so these are the campaign's work list.
This file is SEEDED, not complete: W1 shipped the correlator, W2 classifies
the rest. `--check` is deliberately not wired into `just check` until then --
a gate that fails on ~2000 rows from the day it lands is one somebody
switches off. Keys beginning with '_' are documentation and are skipped.
the `<lang>:` rows for its own lane, and `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every
shard in this directory. One agent per lane can write without a rebase
conflict against the others.
SHARDED BY TOPIC: this file holds one stage's rows in ALL THREE
languages, because the campaign closes a feature at a time across every
language. `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every shard here, and
`--self-test` rejects a row whose item belongs to a different stage.

c:borrow_loaned_message.why: RFC-0010's zero-copy path. rcl/rclcpp borrow a TYPED message the middleware owns (`LoanedMessage<T>`, `borrow_loaned_message`, `publish_loaned_message`, `return_loaned_message_from_publisher`); ours is a TOKEN over a byte range (`loan`/`commit`/`discard` on the publisher, `borrow`/`release` on the subscription) because C has no templates and the wrapper would need an allocator to own. NOTE the verbs differ as well as the shape, and only the shape has a reason -- W5 should decide whether `loan`/`commit`/`discard` should read `borrow_loaned_message`/`publish_loaned_message`/`return_loaned_message`.

c:client_try_recv_response.why: the service-client half of `try_recv`; recorded here because the topic patterns file `try_recv` under pubsub. See the service stage for the client model.

c:event_publisher_count_cb_t.why: QoS events. rclcpp routes every event through one `set_on_new_qos_event_callback` plus a `QOSEventHandler` waitable the executor polls; ours are named callbacks per event (`on_liveliness_lost`, `on_offered_deadline_missed`, `on_message_lost`) registered on the entity. Constraint: no allocator for a per-event handler object and no wait-set to poll it from -- the callback is a fn-ptr in the entity's own static storage. The set of events is the same. This one reports matched-subscription count changes, which rclcpp answers by POLLING `get_subscription_count` -- see that row.

c:executor_add_subscription_in_group.why: adds a subscription to a named callback group, which rclc has no concept of (rclcpp does -- see `cpp:Node::create_callback_group` in the exec stage). Needed because RFC-0002 maps groups onto RTOS priority tiers.

c:executor_add_subscription_raw_with_inf.why: the raw + message-info form; see `c:publish_raw` and `rust:RawMessageInfo`.

c:get_zero_initialized_publisher.why: rcl's free-function spelling; ours is `nros_publisher_get_zero_initialized`, a method-style name on the type. See `c:get_zero_initialized_node`.

c:get_zero_initialized_subscription_cont.why: content-filtered topics are a DDS feature: the subscriber ships an SQL-ish expression the WRITER evaluates. Only one of our backends is DDS, and the filter would have to be a no-op on zenoh and XRCE -- a QoS-shaped promise two of three transports cannot keep. Same reasoning `rmw-api-parity.py` already records for `rmw_*_content_filter`.

c:message_type_t.why: the typesupport handle a publisher or subscription is created with. rosidl's `rosidl_message_type_support_t` carries function pointers into generated code plus an identifier used to pick a middleware-specific implementation at RUNTIME; ours names the one linked backend's descriptor, because an image has exactly one.

c:publish.why: rcl's free function `rcl_publish(publisher, msg, allocation)`; ours is the method-style `nros_publisher_publish`. The WORD matches; the spelling is ours to align, and it is the same shape as `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`.

c:publisher_get_actual_qos.why: reports the QoS the middleware actually negotiated, which can differ from what was requested. QoS is selected at COMPILE time here and no backend downgrades it at runtime (RFC-0036), so actual and requested are the same value by construction -- an accessor would return its own input.

c:publisher_get_context.why: reaches the context a publisher was created on. There is no separate context object -- see the init stage's `c:context_*`.

c:publisher_get_options.why: reads back the options struct a publisher was created with; there is no options struct (`compile-time-options` rule).

c:publisher_get_rmw_handle.why: hands out the underlying rmw/rcl handle so a caller can bypass the API. Our RMW seam is the vtable in `nros/rmw_vtable.h` (RFC-0035) and is deliberately not reachable from an entity; see `c:node_get_rmw_handle`.

c:publisher_get_subscription_count.why: how many subscriptions are matched, RIGHT NOW. We notify on change (`nros_event_publisher_count_cb_t` + `nros_count_status_t`) and never let a caller ask, so code that wants to skip work when nobody is listening has to keep its own mirror of the callback's last value. Both forms are useful and rclcpp ships both. Phase 379 W3.

c:publisher_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our naming; see `c:node_get_zero_initialized`.

c:publisher_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl. Our handles carry their state inline because there is no allocator to put it behind a pointer; see the init stage's `c:context_*`.

c:publisher_init_best_effort.why: rclc ships a named entry point per QoS preset (`_default`, `_best_effort`). Ours takes a QoS value (`nros_publisher_init_with_qos`) because the presets are a `nros_qos_t` a caller can also build, and a named function per preset does not scale past the two rclc chose.

c:publisher_init_default.why: rclc's convenience wrapper: publisher with the default QoS. `nros_publisher_init` takes no QoS and IS the default form; `nros_publisher_init_with_qos` is the explicit one.

c:subscription_try_recv_raw.why: the ours-only half of the `take` -> `try_recv` rename pair (`c:take`); recorded so the pair is visible from both sides. the ours-only half of the SERIALIZED -> RAW rename pair (`c:take_serialized_message`).

c:subscription_try_recv_validated.why: receive WITH the end-to-end integrity verdict attached (`nros_integrity_status_t`: sequence gap, duplicate, CRC valid/mismatch/absent). RFC-0028. ROS 2 has no counterpart because a desktop DDS link is not treated as a safety channel.

c:take.why: rcl, rclcpp and rclrs all spell the non-blocking receive `take`; we spell it `try_recv`. Both are non-blocking and both report emptiness without failing, so nothing about an RTOS asks for the other word -- and `try_recv` is Rust channel vocabulary that reads as a different contract to a ROS 2 user. Covers `nros_subscription_try_recv{,_raw,_sequence,_validated}` and the C++/Rust spellings. Phase 379 W5.

c:take_sequence.why: batch receive; ours is `nros_subscription_try_recv_sequence`. Same word as `c:take`.

c:take_serialized_message.why: ROS 2 says SERIALIZED for the pre-CDR byte form; we say RAW (`publish_raw`, `try_recv_raw`, `nros_cpp_publisher_publish_raw`). One word, used consistently on both sides, and ours is the one that has to move. Phase 379 W5.

cpp:CallbackGroup::find_subscription_ptr.why: rclcpp's `Waitable` protocol: the executor asks each entity how many wait-set slots it needs, then takes the ready data back out. RFC-0002's executor drives entities directly through the RMW vtable's has_data/drive_io, so there is no wait-set for an entity to describe itself to. Executor plumbing, not pub/sub API.

rust:Node::create_subscription.why: the theirs-only half of the node stage's `rust:Node::create_subscriber` rename -- rclrs, rclcpp, rclc and our own C and C++ all say SUBSCRIPTION. Phase 379 W5.

rust:Node::get_publishers_info_by_topic.why: endpoint discovery: which publishers/subscriptions exist on a topic and with what QoS. Needs dynamic discovery, which we do not have -- peers are static via `nros.toml`/Kconfig. See the graph stage for the rest of this family.

rust:Node::get_subscriptions_info_by_top.why: endpoint discovery: which publishers/subscriptions exist on a topic and with what QoS. Needs dynamic discovery, which we do not have -- peers are static via `nros.toml`/Kconfig. See the graph stage for the rest of this family.

rust:Node::publisher_count.why: how many publishers this node DECLARED -- a property of the declaration, not of the graph. rclrs's `count_publishers` asks the graph about a topic; the two answer different questions and only ours works without discovery.

rust:NodeSubscriptionCallback.why: rclrs's conversion traits let `create_subscription` accept a plain closure, an async closure or a worker closure and normalise them. Ours binds a NAMED callback at declaration (RFC-0043), so there is one shape and nothing to convert.

rust:Publisher.why: rclrs 0.5 splits every entity into `X` (an `Arc<XState>` alias) and `XState` (the inherent impl); ours is one type. The correlator folds the suffix, so the members listed here are the ones with no counterpart at all -- see `rust:PublisherState::get_subscription_count` and the loan rows.

rust:Publisher::assert_liveliness.why: manual liveliness assertion. rclcpp has `PublisherBase::assert_liveliness`, which folds onto ours by the *Base rule; recorded here because the Rust side has no rclrs counterpart -- rclrs does not expose liveliness at all.

rust:Publisher::buffer_error.why: constructs the error for a too-small serialisation buffer -- part of the caller-supplied-buffer contract in `rust:Publisher::publish`. rclrs owns the buffer and cannot fail this way.

rust:Publisher::notify_on_subscriber_rea.why: rclrs's async wait for the first matched subscription. Needs a future and a runtime to await it; the event form is `register_event_callback` (see the QoS-event rows).

rust:Publisher::publish.why: ours is `publish(&self, msg: &M, buf: &mut [u8])`; rclrs takes the message by value and serialises into a buffer it owns. The caller supplies the serialisation buffer because there is no allocator, and it is `&M` rather than `M` because a no_std caller usually wants to keep the message. This is the `no-allocator` constraint at the hottest call in the API.

rust:Publisher::publish_raw.why: the ours-only half of the SERIALIZED -> RAW rename pair (`c:take_serialized_message`).

rust:Publisher::register_event_callback.why: QoS events. rclcpp routes every event through one `set_on_new_qos_event_callback` plus a `QOSEventHandler` waitable the executor polls; ours are named callbacks per event (`on_liveliness_lost`, `on_offered_deadline_missed`, `on_message_lost`) registered on the entity. Constraint: no allocator for a per-event handler object and no wait-set to poll it from -- the callback is a fn-ptr in the entity's own static storage. The set of events is the same.

rust:Publisher::supports_event.why: asks whether the linked backend raises a given QoS event, because they differ: zenoh-pico raises no deadline events and Cyclone does. rclcpp assumes DDS and always claims support.

rust:Publisher::topic_name.why: reads back the topic a publisher was created on. C and C++ have it (`nros_publisher_get_topic_name`, `Publisher::get_topic_name`); the Rust publisher does not, so the three languages disagree with each other as well as with ROS 2. Phase 379 W3.

rust:Publisher::unsupported_event_error.why: the error `supports_event` predicts; see that row.

rust:PublisherGid.why: rclrs wraps the GID in a type; ours is a fixed array plus `PUBLISHER_GID_SIZE`, because a wrapper with no allocator buys only the name.

rust:PublisherHandle.why: the backend-agnostic publisher a component holds. rclrs's `Publisher` IS the rcl handle; ours is an index into the executor's static entity table, because the entity outlives the borrow that created it.

rust:PublisherOptions::qos.why: ours carries QoS and nothing else; rclrs's publisher options also carry the callback group and the allocator. See `compile-time-options`.

rust:RawMessageInfo.why: message metadata plus the transport ATTACHMENT (zenoh carries source timestamp and publisher GID there rather than in the payload). rclrs has `MessageInfo` and no attachment because DDS has no such field.

rust:RawSubscriptionCallback.why: the raw-bytes callback type. See `c:subscription_callback_t` -- bound at declaration, not handed to an executor.

rust:ReadOnlyLoanedMessage.why: RFC-0010's zero-copy path. rcl/rclcpp borrow a TYPED message the middleware owns (`LoanedMessage<T>`, `borrow_loaned_message`, `publish_loaned_message`, `return_loaned_message_from_publisher`); ours is a TOKEN over a byte range (`loan`/`commit`/`discard` on the publisher, `borrow`/`release` on the subscription) because C has no templates and the wrapper would need an allocator to own. NOTE the verbs differ as well as the shape, and only the shape has a reason -- W5 should decide whether `loan`/`commit`/`discard` should read `borrow_loaned_message`/`publish_loaned_message`/`return_loaned_message`. rclrs splits read-only from writable loans by type; ours is one borrow with a const view.

rust:Session::create_publisher.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend. Exported from `nros::` alongside the user API, which is issue 0784's complaint.

rust:Subscription::has_data.why: non-destructive readiness check, so a caller can decide whether to take without taking. rclrs's executor answers this through the wait set; a polling caller has no wait set. See `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

rust:Subscription::process_raw_in_place.why: hands the callback the received bytes in the transport's own buffer, with no copy into caller storage. RFC-0010's zero-copy path on the receive side for backends that can hold the buffer across the call; `supports_process_in_place` says which can.

rust:Subscription::register_event_callba.why: QoS events. rclcpp routes every event through one `set_on_new_qos_event_callback` plus a `QOSEventHandler` waitable the executor polls; ours are named callbacks per event (`on_liveliness_lost`, `on_offered_deadline_missed`, `on_message_lost`) registered on the entity. Constraint: no allocator for a per-event handler object and no wait-set to poll it from -- the callback is a fn-ptr in the entity's own static storage. The set of events is the same.

Ours binds a NAMED callback at declaration (RFC-0043), so there is one shape and nothing to convert. The async form additionally needs a runtime.
